claims.text: A machine-learned surrogate trained on ab initio free-energy data for solid and fluid phases can accurately predict fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties of multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The surrogate can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The surrogate will have substantially lower computational cost than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
The model will be trained on elemental and binary ab initio free-energy calculations and then applied to multicomponent HEAs.
The training free energies will include vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The intended composition domain consists of HEAs with 3–5 principal elements, each present at 5–35 at%.
The intended temperature domain is 0.8–1.2 times the expected melting point.
A model trained only on elemental and binary systems can interpolate or extrapolate to multicomponent systems.
The surrogate will capture local atomic environments and their contributions to free energy in both solid and fluid phases.
The learned local-environment representation will capture vibrational and electronic effects.
Learning a mapping from atomic configuration and composition to free energy will bypass costly molecular-dynamics sampling during prediction.
By bypassing molecular-dynamics sampling, the surrogate will enable rapid evaluation of phase free energies and derived fusion properties.
Predicted melting point, latent heat, entropy change, and other high-temperature observables will be within 5–10% of explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD results.
The surrogate will reduce computational cost by 10–100 times for multicomponent HEAs.
Explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD are accurate but computationally expensive, particularly for multicomponent alloys.
The hypothesis is expected to hold when the HEA local environments are sufficiently represented by elemental and binary training data.
The method may fail for compositions or temperatures that produce local structures absent from the training data.
The hypothesis is falsified if fusion-property errors exceed 10% relative to explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD, or if the cost reduction is less than tenfold.
